headline: Amazon cuts 1,300 jobs
text: On January 30 Amazon reported fourth-quarter sales of $972 million, up 44%, and 2000 sales of $2.76 billion. The quarter's net loss was $545 million, including $339 million of write-downs on goodwill and investments in other internet companies. It is cutting about 1,300 jobs, 15% of its workforce, closing a distribution centre in Georgia and running its Seattle centre only in season.
imageCaption: Jeff Bezos in 1999, when Amazon was adding music, video, games and gifts to its books

headline: A surprise rate cut: the Nasdaq jumps 14% in a day
text: On 3 January the Federal Reserve cut interest rates by half a point, from 6.5% to 6%, without waiting for its next meeting. The Nasdaq rose 14.17% that day to 2,616.69, its biggest gain ever, and 12% over the month. Beaten-down technology shares rebounded hardest: Microsoft rose about 41% in January, Apple 45%.
imageCaption: Alan Greenspan, chairman of the Federal Reserve, at the IMF meetings in Prague, September 2000

headline: eBay doubles revenue and stays profitable
text: eBay's revenue for 2000 rose to $431 million from $225 million and net income to $48 million. It has 22.5 million registered users. In January it agreed to buy a majority of Internet Auction, the leading auction site in South Korea, and announced higher fees in the United States from January 31.
imageCaption: Meg Whitman, eBay's chief executive

headline: IBM beats forecasts as the Fed starts cutting
text: IBM earned 1.48 dollars a share in the fourth quarter, up 32%, slightly above analysts' 1.46, on revenue of 25.6 billion dollars. Full-year 2000 profit rose 16% to 8.1 billion dollars. The Federal Reserve cut its key rate twice in January, on the 3rd and the 31st, by half a point each time.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000051143/000091205701001854/a2035335zex-99_1.txt (IBM results release of 2001-01-17, read 2026-10-03); https://money.cnn.com/2001/01/17/technology/earns_ibm/ (analyst estimate of $1.46, via search result, read 2026-10-03); https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/openmarket_archive.htm (read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: An IBM System/390 Multiprise 3000 server

headline: Nestlé agrees to buy Ralston Purina
text: Nestlé and the American pet food maker Ralston Purina agreed a merger in January: Nestlé will pay $33.50 a share in cash, an enterprise value of $10.3 billion. Ralston brings Dog Chow, Cat Chow and the Purina brands, to be combined with Nestlé's Friskies. Competition authorities still have to approve.
imageCaption: St. Louis skyline with the headquarters of Purina Mills at the extreme left

headline: The Fed cuts by half a point, twice in one month
text: On 3 January, in an unscheduled move, the Fed cut its rate target by half a point to 6 percent, citing weakening sales and production, falling consumer confidence and high energy prices. At its meeting at the end of the month it cut by another half point, to 5.5 percent. As recently as May 2000 it had raised the rate to 6.5 percent to cool the boom.
imageCaption: Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan testifies to the Senate Budget Committee, Washington, 25 January 2001

headline: Greece becomes the twelfth euro country
text: On 1 January Greece adopted the euro, two years after the first eleven countries. In 1998 it had failed the entry tests; in June 2000 the EU judged that it now meets them and fixed the rate at 340.75 drachmas per euro. Like Italy and Belgium, Greece owes more than its whole annual economic output, far above the 60 percent limit in the rules. Euro notes and coins are to follow in all twelve countries in January 2002.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enlargement_of_the_eurozone (read 2026-10-04); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euro_convergence_criteria (read 2026-10-04); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_euro (read 2026-10-04); European Monetary Institute, Convergence Report, March 1998, https://www.ecb.europa.eu/pub/pdf/conrep/cr1998en.pdf (read 2026-10-04); Eurostat, Report on the revision of the Greek government deficit and debt figures, 22 November 2004, https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/4187653/5765001/GREECE-EN.PDF (read 2026-10-04)

headline: Cisco misses for the first time in years
text: Cisco reported on February 6 that sales in the quarter to January 27 rose 55% to $6.75 billion, but the result fell short of analysts' expectations, the company's first miss after years of beating forecasts. Chief executive John Chambers spoke of 'a brief pause in the current 10-year expansion of the U.S. economy' but said he remained confident about the next three to five years.
imageCaption: Fortune's cover of 15 May 2000, nine months before the miss: 'Is John Chambers the best CEO on earth? Is it too late to buy his stock?'
imageCredit: Fortune magazine cover (photograph of the printed copy, not credited on the page)

headline: Schlumberger bets 5 billion dollars on information technology
text: On 12 February Schlumberger offered 560 pence in cash a share, an 18 percent premium, for Sema plc, a British-French IT services company, valuing it at about 5.2 billion dollars. It dwarfs its earlier purchases, such as the 2.2 billion dollar Camco deal of 1998. Its shares fell 17 percent this month.
imageCaption: Schlumberger's Solutions Center office tower, Houston

headline: The telecom bust: network gear makers crash
text: The Nasdaq fell 22% in February to 2,152, its lowest since late 1998. Telephone companies, which have borrowed heavily to build fibre-optic and mobile networks and paid billions for mobile licences in Europe, are cutting orders, and the makers of their equipment warn of falling sales. Cisco lost more than a third in February, and the makers of optical parts for the networks fared worse.
imageCaption: Lucent Technologies' headquarters at Murray Hill, New Jersey

headline: Skilling takes over; 'most innovative' for the sixth year
text: Jeffrey Skilling took over as Enron's chief executive on 12 February. Fortune magazine named Enron America's most innovative company for the sixth year in a row.
imageCaption: Jeffrey Skilling, president and chief operating officer of Enron, 1999

headline: Earnings disappoint and shares fall 9 percent despite Fed cuts
text: A steady flow of disappointing company earnings reports sent shares sharply lower in February, with the technology-heavy Nasdaq falling hardest, and consumer confidence dropped. The Federal Reserve had already cut its key rate twice in January, including a surprise move on 3 January. The S&P 500 lost 9% in the month to 1,239.94.
imageCaption: Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan testifies to the Senate Banking Committee, Washington, 13 February 2001
imageCredit: Photo by MARIO TAMA/AFP via Getty Images

headline: Philip Morris was the best Dow stock of 2000
text: Philip Morris shares gained 90% in 2000, the best performance among the 30 Dow Jones stocks in a year when most indexes fell; at about 46 dollars they are more than twice their level of January 2000. The company earned 8.5 billion dollars in 2000. Investors expect the Engle verdict to be overturned, think the new Bush administration will be gentler on tobacco, and like a business that sells in any economy as technology stocks crash.
imageCaption: The trading floor of the New York Stock Exchange

headline: Nokia slides as the phone market slows
text: On 30 January Nokia cut its first-quarter sales growth forecast to 25-30% and its estimate for world phone sales this year to 500-550 million, citing economic uncertainty and slowing phone sales; earlier in January it had disclosed lower 2000 phone sales than analysts hoped. Wireless shares have been under pressure on signs of slowing growth and falling profitability. Nokia's ADR lost 36% in February.
imageCaption: Nokia 9210, 7650, 6250 and 6310 handsets

headline: Cisco announces the first layoffs in its history
text: On March 9 Cisco said it will cut 2,500 to 3,000 temporary and contract workers and 3,000 to 5,000 of its 44,000 regular employees, and take a charge of $300 million to $400 million. Chambers blamed 'the continuing slowdown in the U.S. economy and initial signs of a slowdown expanding to other parts of the world.' Only a year ago, on March 27, 2000, Cisco was worth $555 billion, more than any other company in the world.
imageCaption: Building 10, the headquarters block of Cisco's San Jose campus

headline: Fortune asks: is Enron overpriced?
text: In an article headlined 'Is Enron Overpriced?', Fortune's Bethany McLean asked how Enron justifies a share price of 55 times earnings when analysts and investors cannot say how it makes its money; she pointed to rising debt and erratic cash flow. Finance chief Andrew Fastow told the magazine Enron does not want anyone to know what is on its trading books. On 9 March Enron and Blockbuster ended their 20-year movies-on-demand deal after eight months.
imageCaption: The Enron Center towers in downtown Houston

headline: Cisco warns sales will fall and cuts 8,500 jobs
text: On April 16 Cisco said sales in the quarter to April will be about $4.7 billion, below the year before, after $6.7 billion in the previous quarter. It raised its job cuts to 8,500 and expects restructuring charges of $800 million to $1.2 billion. Chambers said the slowdown 'may be the fastest any industry our size has ever decelerated.'
imageCaption: Cisco Ethernet and ATM fibre modules
imageCredit: Cisco Systems (Center for Cisco Heritage archive, Computer History Museum)

headline: Amazon's losses narrow
text: Amazon reported first-quarter sales of $700 million, up 22% from a year earlier. Technology shares rallied in April after months of falls.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1018724/000095010901500823/d10q.htm (10-Q for the quarter to March 31, 2001, read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: Jeff Bezos (black shirt) with the Amazon toys team at the company summer picnic, 2000

headline: eBay's revenue up 79%
text: eBay's revenue for the first quarter rose 79% to $154 million from $86 million a year earlier, helped by more users and listings and by the fee increases of January 31.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1065088/000109581101502243/f72456e10-q.txt (10-Q for the quarter to March 31, 2001, read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: eBay's headquarters in San Jose, California

headline: Skilling insults an analyst on a conference call
text: Enron reported record recurring earnings of 47 cents a share for the first quarter and raised its outlook for 2001. On the conference call, when analyst Richard Grubman complained that Enron was the only company that could not release a balance sheet with its earnings, chief executive Jeffrey Skilling called him an obscenity.
imageCaption: Jeffrey Skilling, chief executive of Enron, in the company's annual report

headline: Cisco writes off $2.2 billion of inventory
text: Cisco reported on May 8 a net loss of $2.69 billion for the quarter to April, on sales of $4.73 billion, down 4% from a year earlier. The loss includes a $2.2 billion charge for excess inventory and $1.17 billion of restructuring costs. Chambers said bookings went from growth of more than 70% in November to a decline of 30% within a few months.
imageCaption: Cisco ONS 15454 optical systems in a rack
imageCredit: Cisco Systems (Center for Cisco Heritage archive, Computer History Museum)

headline: Glivec: a cancer pill approved in record time
text: The US Food and Drug Administration approved Novartis's imatinib, sold as Gleevec in the US and Glivec elsewhere, for a form of leukaemia, only two and a half years after the application. Time magazine put it on its cover as a new weapon against cancer. It will cost about $30,000 a year.
imageCaption: 'There is new ammunition in the war against cancer. These are the bullets': TIME's cover on Gleevec (Glivec), 28 May 2001

headline: Kraft goes public in the second-largest IPO ever
text: Philip Morris sold about 16% of Kraft Foods to the public in June, raising 8.7 billion dollars in the second-largest initial public offering to date; it keeps 84% of the shares and 98% of the votes. Kraft now includes Nabisco, the maker of Oreo and Ritz, which Philip Morris bought in 2000 for 55 dollars a share in cash, an enterprise value of 18.9 billion dollars. It is the largest food company in North America.
source: https://www.referenceforbusiness.com/history2/72/Philip-Morris-Companies-Inc.html (read 2026-10-03); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/764180/000095013000003538/0000950130-00-003538-0002.txt (Nabisco terms, Philip Morris 8-K of 26 June 2000, read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: Kraft macaroni and cheese, one of Kraft's best-known products

headline: Appeals court throws out the breakup
text: On 28 June the federal appeals court in Washington upheld part of the finding that Microsoft illegally maintained its monopoly, but overturned the order to break up the company and sent the case back to a new judge.
imageCaption: The federal courthouse in Washington, home of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit

headline: Nokia warns again as the slowdown spreads
text: On 12 June Nokia warned that second-quarter earnings will be 0.15-0.17 euros a share, below expectations, that sales growth will be under 10%, and that it will take a restructuring charge, citing the spread of the US slowdown and less aggressive marketing by operators. Its ADR fell nearly 20% that day.
imageCaption: The Nokia 3330, 2001

headline: The new Mini goes on sale
text: BMW's new Mini, built at the former Morris plant in Cowley, Oxford, went on sale in July. It is the first new car of BMW's 'premium only' strategy after the sale of Rover and Land Rover: a small car sold at a high price on the strength of a famous name.
imageCaption: The new Mini One, 2001

headline: Europe blocks the Honeywell deal
text: On 3 July the European Commission, under competition commissioner Mario Monti, blocked General Electric's takeover of Honeywell, although US authorities had cleared it. Brussels feared GE could bundle its jet engines, aircraft leasing and Honeywell's avionics to squeeze out rivals.
imageCaption: Mario Monti, the European Commissioner for Competition
imageCredit: Christian Lambiotte, European Commission Audiovisual Service

headline: Young Roger Federer beats Sampras at Wimbledon
text: The 19-year-old Roger Federer of Basel beat Pete Sampras, the four-time defending champion, in five sets in the fourth round at Wimbledon, ending Sampras's run of 31 wins there. Federer then lost in the quarter-finals. He was Wimbledon junior champion in 1998.
imageCaption: Roger Federer and Pete Sampras shake hands after their fourth-round match, Wimbledon, 2 July 2001
imageCredit: photo agency picture via tennisworldusa.org (photographer not named)

headline: Skilling quits after six months
text: Jeffrey Skilling resigned as Enron's chief executive on 14 August after six months, citing personal reasons; Kenneth Lay takes the job back. Lay told analysts there were 'no accounting issues, no trading issues' and that the company was in the strongest shape it had ever been in. The shares hit a 52-week low; Skilling had sold shares worth about $33 million in the months before.
imageCaption: Jeffrey Skilling (left) and Kenneth Lay of Enron, 1999

headline: Terror with Boeing jets; up to 30,000 jobs to go
text: On 11 September hijackers flew four Boeing jets, two 767s and two 757s, into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and a field in Pennsylvania. With airlines cutting flights, Boeing said on 18 September it will reduce its airliner workforce by 20,000 to 30,000 by the end of 2002.
imageCaption: Smoke rising from the World Trade Center, seen from across the river, New York, 11 September 2001

headline: The September attacks empty Disney's parks; the Bass family sells
text: After the attacks of 11 September air travel stopped and stock exchanges closed until 17 September. Tourism-dependent companies such as Disney were hit hard. On 20 September Disney said it had bought 50 million of its own shares from 'certain significant stockholders' at a discount, and Goldman Sachs bought another 85 million to resell; the Texas billionaire Sid Bass, a large Disney shareholder since 1984, was forced to sell his holdings to meet a margin call.
imageCaption: Sleeping Beauty Castle, Disneyland, Anaheim

headline: Immelt takes over as terror strikes
text: Jeff Immelt, the former head of GE Medical Systems, has succeeded Jack Welch as chairman and chief executive. Within days of the handover, the terror attacks of 11 September hit GE's airline and insurance customers. Welch leaves after twenty years in which GE's market value rose from about 14 billion to more than 400 billion dollars.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Immelt (read 2026-10-03); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/40545/000095013002001437/ddef14a.txt (GE proxy 2002, read 2026-10-03); https://www.ge.com/news/reports/jack-welch-the-ultimate-manager-who-oversaw-ges-rise-to-the-most-valuable-company-dies-at-84 (read 2026-10-03, $14 billion to $410 billion)
imageCaption: Jack Welch (left) and Jeffrey Immelt at the press conference naming Immelt his successor, New York, November 2000

headline: After the attacks: markets closed four days, then the worst week in decades
text: The New York Stock Exchange stayed closed after the terrorist attacks of 11 September and reopened only on 17 September, its longest closure since the Great Depression. That day the Fed cut its key rate to 3 percent, and the Dow fell 684.81 points or 7.1%; shares kept falling in volatile trading as business and consumer confidence collapsed. The S&P 500 lost 8% in September to 1,040.94.
imageCaption: A trader looks up grimly at a screen as the New York Stock Exchange reopens, 17 September 2001

headline: Attacks on New York and Washington; Wall Street's worst week since the 1930s
text: On 11 September hijackers flew airliners into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon, and a fourth plane crashed in Pennsylvania; thousands are dead or missing. US stock markets stayed shut until 17 September, when the Dow fell 684 points, 7.1 percent, its biggest one-day point loss, and ended the week down more than 14 percent; airline and insurance shares were hit hardest. In Tehran, people held candlelight vigils for the victims, and President Khatami sent his sympathy.
imageCaption: On the floor of the New York Stock Exchange, a trader comforts another during the moment of silence before trading resumes, 17 September 2001
imageCredit: David L Ryan | Boston Globe | Getty Images

headline: Terror attacks on New York and Washington
text: On 11 September nineteen hijackers seized four airliners; two destroyed the twin towers of the World Trade Center in New York, one hit the Pentagon and one crashed in Pennsylvania. Thousands are dead. Al-Qaeda, led by Osama bin Laden, is blamed. The New York Stock Exchange stayed closed until 17 September, when the Dow fell 684 points, or 7.1 percent, its largest point fall ever; airline, insurance and travel shares fell hardest. Congress voted 15 billion dollars of aid for the airlines, and NATO invoked its mutual-defence clause for the first time.
imageCaption: Smoke pours from the twin towers of the World Trade Center after the attacks, New York, 11 September 2001

headline: September 11 brings the biggest insurance loss ever
text: The attacks of 11 September have caused the largest insured loss in history, estimated at around 40 billion dollars for the industry. Berkshire, through General Re and its other reinsurers, is expected to be among the largest payers, with losses of more than 2 billion dollars. Stock exchanges were closed until 17 September.
imageCaption: Smoke over Lower Manhattan seen from the International Space Station, 11 September 2001

headline: Terror attacks hit insurers and banks
text: After the attacks of 11 September in the US, European share markets plunged; insurance shares were among the hardest hit, falling about 15% on the day in Frankfurt. Credit Suisse owns the insurer Winterthur. By 28 September the Swiss Market Index had recovered from about 5,000 to 6,000 in five days, but the broad SPI is still almost 28% below its level at the end of 2000.
source: Neue Zürcher Zeitung, 29 September 2001, p. 33 ('Der DAX schöpft neuen Mut'; 'Der schweizerische Aktienmarkt: In fünf Tagen von 5000 auf 6000'), scan data/manual/scans/nzz/NZZ_2001-09-29.pdf (read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: Smoke over lower Manhattan after the attacks on the World Trade Center, New York, 11 September 2001

headline: Enron 'trading under a cloud'
text: Investors are struggling to understand Enron's accounts; one prominent hedge fund manager said the stock was trading under a cloud. The company admits to deals with 'related parties', some of them partnerships run by its finance chief Andrew Fastow. After the 11 September attacks the stock market fell sharply, and Enron's shares lost more than a fifth in the month.
imageCaption: The skybridge between the Enron Center towers, downtown Houston

headline: Terror attack drives Lehman from its headquarters
text: The 11 September attacks severely damaged Lehman's headquarters at Three World Financial Center, across the street from the World Trade Center, and displaced more than 6,500 employees; one Lehman employee was killed. The firm moved its trading to Jersey City and was trading again when markets reopened on 17 September. Its third-quarter profit fell to $309 million from $457 million.
imageCaption: The World Financial Center towers and the Marriott at the World Trade Center, 2 September 2001

headline: The September 11 attacks hit DaimlerChrysler
text: After the terrorist attacks of 11 September, the New York Stock Exchange stayed closed until 17 September; when it reopened the Dow fell 14% in a week. DaimlerChrysler earns much of its money in the United States, where Chrysler is already losing heavily.
imageCaption: Smoke over Lower Manhattan after the attacks, seen from the International Space Station, 11 September 2001

headline: Markets slump after the September 11 attacks
text: After the attacks of 11 September, US stock exchanges stayed closed until 17 September; on reopening the Dow fell 7.1% in a day. European markets fell with them. Siemens shares lost a quarter of their value in September.
imageCaption: The ruins of the World Trade Center, New York, 14 September 2001

headline: The iPod: a thousand songs in your pocket
text: Apple introduced the iPod, a portable music player with a 5-gigabyte hard disk that holds about 1,000 songs and works with Apple's iTunes software on the Mac.
imageCaption: The first iPod, with its earphones and charger, as Apple presented it on 23 October 2001

headline: Enron loses $618 million; SEC asks questions; finance chief out
text: On 16 October Enron reported a third-quarter loss of $618 million after $1.01 billion of charges on its water, broadband and other ventures, and cut shareholders' equity by $1.2 billion over deals with partnerships run by finance chief Andrew Fastow. On 22 October it disclosed an SEC inquiry and the shares fell $5.40 to $20.65 in a day; Fastow was replaced on 24 October. Enron drew on its bank credit lines to repay $3.3 billion of commercial paper, and Moody's cut its credit rating.
imageCaption: Kenneth Lay, chairman of Enron, 1999

headline: Swissair grounded
text: On 2 October Swissair grounded its entire fleet when fuel suppliers refused to fill its planes without cash and UBS would not release a bridging loan for daily operations; thousands of passengers were stranded around the world. Federal President Moritz Leuenberger called it a disaster and blamed UBS and Credit Suisse for abandoning the airline, and angry crowds protested at the UBS headquarters. The government granted a bridging loan of 450 million francs on 3 October so that flights could resume, and a new airline is to be built around Crossair. On 7 October the United States began bombing Afghanistan.
imageCaption: Swissair's fleet stands grounded at Zurich-Kloten airport, 2 October 2001

headline: Swissair grounded
text: On 2 October the entire Swissair fleet was grounded after UBS refused to extend its credit line. UBS and Credit Suisse bought SAirGroup's stake in Crossair, which is to take over Swissair's European flights, and federal bridge loans let flights resume on 5 October. Lukas Mühlemann, chairman of Credit Suisse, sat on the Swissair board during its troubles.
imageCaption: Grounded Swissair aircraft at Zurich airport, 2 October 2001

headline: Apple's iPod: '1,000 songs in your pocket'
text: On 23 October Apple presented the iPod, a music player with a 5 GB hard drive that holds about 1,000 songs, works with Apple's iTunes software on the Mac, and is controlled with a scroll wheel. It goes on sale on 10 November for 399 dollars, a lot for a music player.
imageCaption: The first-generation iPod, presented on 23 October 2001: '1,000 songs in your pocket'

headline: Nokia's results beat fears
text: On 19 October Nokia said third-quarter profit before one-off items fell 18% to 760 million euros, better than the 25% fall analysts expected, and forecast fourth-quarter earnings of 0.18-0.20 euros a share. Its shares rose.
imageCaption: The Nokia 7650, the company's first camera phone

headline: Swissair grounded; the banks are blamed
text: On 2 October the entire Swissair fleet was grounded after UBS refused to extend its credit line to the indebted airline. Many Swiss blamed UBS; demonstrators carried signs calling chairman Marcel Ospel 'Bin Ospel'. UBS and Credit Suisse bought SAirGroup's stake in Crossair, which is to take over Swissair's European flights, and the federal government lent money so that flights could resume on 5 October.
imageCaption: About 400 Swissair employees protest outside the UBS head office on the Paradeplatz, Zurich, 3 October 2001

headline: Dynegy rescue collapses; Enron cut to junk
text: Enron admitted it had overstated profits since 1997 by about $590 million and agreed on 9 November to be taken over by its smaller Houston rival Dynegy for about $8 billion in stock. A filing on 19 November showed about $9 billion of debt due by the end of 2002 and warned of the risk to Enron's survival. On 28 November the rating agencies cut Enron to junk, making $3.9 billion of debt due at once, and Dynegy walked away; the shares closed at 61 cents.
imageCaption: Wells Fargo Bank Plaza, 1000 Louisiana Street, Houston, headquarters of Dynegy

headline: Cisco's sales grow again from the previous quarter
text: Cisco reported on November 5 sales of $4.4 billion for the quarter to October, 32% below a year earlier but 3% above the previous quarter, and a small profit before special charges. Chambers said the company gained market share while competitors' sales fell by high-teens percentages.
imageCaption: Cisco's San Jose campus, Building 2 and the company sign

headline: Settlement with the government, and the Xbox launches
text: On 1 November the Justice Department, which said in September it would no longer seek a breakup, reached a settlement with Microsoft: Microsoft must share its programming interfaces with other companies and accept a monitoring panel for five years. On 15 November Microsoft launched the Xbox, its first games console, in North America.
imageCaption: The original Xbox console, launched 15 November 2001

headline: The Xbox goes on sale with Nvidia inside
text: Microsoft launched the Xbox in North America on 15 November, with graphics and media processors from Nvidia; commercial shipments of the chips began in July. Nvidia's shares have more than doubled this year.
imageCaption: The original Xbox console and controllers, 2001

headline: Enron files for bankruptcy, the largest in U.S. history
text: Enron filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection on 2 December, the largest corporate bankruptcy in U.S. history, with debts of about $31 billion. It laid off 4,000 employees in Houston and sued Dynegy for $10 billion. Many employees held most of their retirement savings in Enron stock, now worth cents; the shares still trade, but shareholders stand behind all creditors.
imageCaption: The tilted E of Enron's logo glows in front of the company's new Houston headquarters on 29 November 2001, the day after the Dynegy rescue collapsed and three days before the bankruptcy filing

headline: China joins the World Trade Organization
text: China became a member of the World Trade Organization on 11 December, after approval at the meeting in Doha in November. China has cut tariffs and promised to open its markets, and it gets lasting access to the markets of the other members. US-China trade was under $100 billion in 1999.
imageCaption: A man walks past a billboard welcoming China's membership of the World Trade Organization, Beijing, 10 December 2001
imageCredit: Photo by GOH Chai Hin / AFP via Getty Images

headline: 2001 in review: eleven rate cuts cannot stop a second losing year
text: The S&P 500 fell 13% in 2001 to 1,148.08 and the Dow 7.1%, a second losing year in a row. The Federal Reserve cut its key rate eleven times during the year, from 6.5 to 1.75 percent, as the economy fell into recession and the September attacks shook confidence.
imageCaption: Traders on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange watch the Dow climb back over 10,000, 5 December 2001
imageCredit: Photo by HENNY RAY ABRAMS/AFP via Getty Images
